lessons.title: Run Ruby source and inspect the runtime
lessons.summary: Change Ready to Changed, save, and run ruby main.rb again. What prints?
explanation: Save the complete example as main.rb and run ruby main.rb using an installed Ruby interpreter. This course verifies Ruby 4.0.9; the app itself supplies reading and checks, not a Ruby browser runner.
Running this command again executes the saved source. You do not manually rebuild a separate executable as in the C examples.
ruby --version reports the runtime. Some libraries are separate gems or native extensions, so a Ruby version alone does not prove that every require will succeed.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
puts "Ready"
```
Expected output or behavior: Ready. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Values are objects with classes
lessons.summary: Replace 7 with "7". What prints?
explanation: An integer, string, true, false and nil are all objects. A value’s class describes its kind of object.
value.class calls the method named class on that value. A method is a named operation an object can respond to; this call reports Integer or String here.
An ordinary local variable can later refer to an object of another class. Reassignment is different from modifying the original object.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
value = 7
puts value.class
```
Expected output or behavior: Integer. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Integer and floating arithmetic
lessons.summary: Replace 5 with 5.0. What prints?
explanation: With two Integer operands, 5 / 2 produces integer 2. For negative results, integer division rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero.
5.0 / 2 produces floating-point 2.5. Floating numbers have finite precision and are not exact decimal-money values.
Ruby Integer can grow beyond a machine-sized integer, subject to available memory. That does not make Float exact or unlimited.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
puts 5 / 2
```
Expected output or behavior: 2. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Truthiness nil and short-circuit choices
lessons.summary: Replace 0 with nil. What prints?
explanation: Only nil and false are false-like in Ruby conditions. Ruby treats 0, the empty string and empty arrays as true in a condition. Do not import another language’s truthiness rules.
nil is a real object used for an absent value; it is distinct from false and from zero.
&& stops after a false-like left operand; || stops after a truthy left operand. They return an operand value, not necessarily true or false.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
value = 0
if value
  puts "present"
else
  puts "absent"
end
```
Expected output or behavior: present. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: String interpolation and quoting
lessons.summary: Change the greeting to single quotes: 'Hello #{name}'. What prints?
explanation: "Hello #{name}" inserts the value of name into a double-quoted string. The #{...} part contains an expression.
A single-quoted string normally treats #{name} as literal text instead of evaluating it. Double quotes also interpret escapes such as \n.
puts writes the string and a line ending. Interpolation does not rename or assign the variable.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
name = "Mira"
puts "Hello #{name}"
```
Expected output or behavior: Hello Mira. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Assignment aliasing and mutation
lessons.summary: Replace other = values with other = values.dup. What prints?
explanation: [1, 2] creates an Array containing two elements. After other = values, both names refer to the same Array object. Assignment does not recursively copy its elements.
other << 3 appends to that shared array. The << method is written like an operator here.
values.dup makes a separate outer Array. It still shares any nested mutable objects, so this simple scalar example is not a deep-copy guarantee.
inspect returns text representing an object; puts writes that text. Here the array representation includes brackets and entries.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
values = [1, 2]
other = values
other << 3
puts values.inspect
```
Expected output or behavior: [1, 2, 3]. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Contrast rebinding a name with mutating the object shared by two names. You may trace it without a Ruby interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Symbols and named keys
lessons.summary: Replace the lookup key :topic with "topic". What prints?
explanation: A symbol literal such as :topic names a stable Symbol value. It is not the same object type as the String "topic".

hash.fetch(key, "missing") returns the entry if that key exists and otherwise returns the supplied default.

values.fetch(5, "missing") returns the fallback for an absent index. Without a fallback or block, fetch raises IndexError.
-1 selects the last element when one exists. It is not automatically an invalid index.

lessons.title: Hashes defaults and missing keys
lessons.summary: Replace the missing-key read with counts[:stars] = 1. What prints?
explanation: Hash.new(0) creates an empty hash with the default value 0. Missing-key reads return that default.
counts[:stars] can return 0 while counts.size remains 0. size counts stored entries, not prior reads.
counts[:stars] = 1 stores the entry. A mutable shared default such as an Array needs additional care and is not used here.

```ruby
puts counts.size
```

lessons.title: Ranges and endpoint rules
lessons.summary: Change the range to 1...3. What prints?
explanation: 1..3 includes the endpoint 3. 1...3 excludes the endpoint 3. The extra dot changes the boundary rule.
to_a collects this small integer range into an Array. Do not materialize an unbounded or enormous range just to inspect it.
join(",") makes one string containing the entries separated by commas. It does not change the original numeric values.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby

```
Expected output or behavior: 1,2,3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: While loops break and next
lessons.summary: Replace next with break. What prints?
explanation: while count < 3 checks before each iteration. Updating count ensures this example eventually stops.
count += 1 adds one and assigns the result back to count. Here == tests equality, unlike = which assigns a value.
next skips the rest of the current loop iteration. break exits the loop entirely. The increment happens before this example skips anything.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
count = 0
while count < 3
  count += 1
  if count == 2
    next
  end
  puts count
end
```

Expected output or behavior: 1
3. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Case selection and matching rules
lessons.summary: Change the when range to 1...3. What prints?
explanation: case value followed by when pattern uses the pattern’s === method to decide whether that branch matches.
For this integer example, 1..3 matches 3 while 1...3 does not. An else branch handles remaining inputs.
After a matching branch is selected, Ruby does not automatically execute the following when branch as C-style switch fallthrough.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
value = 3
case value
when 1..3
  puts "inside"
else
  puts "outside"
end
```
Expected output or behavior: inside. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Method results and local scope
lessons.summary: Change the method expression to score = 9. What prints?
explanation: A method defined with def does not automatically read an outer local variable just because it has the same name.
Ruby methods normally return their last evaluated expression. return can also leave a method explicitly.
A parameter is a local name for the argument object. Rebinding that name is different from mutating a shared mutable argument.

```ruby
def shown(score)
  score + 1
end
puts shown(score)
puts score
```

lessons.title: Defaults and keyword arguments
lessons.summary: Also supply prefix: "Explore". What prints?
explanation: A parameter can declare a default value. The caller can supply another value instead.
def label(topic:, prefix: "Study") requires topic and gives prefix a default. label(topic: "stars") passes a keyword, not a positional hash automatically.
A missing required keyword or an unaccepted keyword raises ArgumentError. Renaming a parameter may affect callers.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
def label(topic:, prefix: "Study")
  "#{prefix}: #{topic}"
end
puts label(topic: "stars")
```
Expected output or behavior: Study: stars. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Rest arguments and keyword forwarding
lessons.summary: Replace settings with an empty hash. What prints?
explanation: *values in a method definition gathers extra positional arguments into an Array.
**options gathers keywords into a Hash. At a call, *numbers expands an Array as positional arguments and **settings expands a Hash as keywords.
options.fetch(:scale, 1) uses one when scale is absent. values.sum adds the numeric entries, starting at zero for an empty array.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
def total(*values, **options)
  values.sum * options.fetch(:scale, 1)
end
numbers = [2, 4]
settings = {scale: 2}
puts total(*numbers, **settings)
```
Expected output or behavior: 12. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compare positional expansion with keyword expansion instead of assuming every trailing hash is a keyword list. You may trace it without a Ruby interpreter; reading completion is not proof of a local run.

lessons.title: Yield and optional blocks
lessons.summary: Remove the block from the adjust(3) call. What prints?
explanation: adjust(3) { |value| value * 2 } supplies a block. The names between vertical bars receive values yielded by the method.
yield value calls the block with value and evaluates to the block’s result. Yielding without a block raises LocalJumpError.
block_given? lets a method choose a no-block path. This method returns the original value when no block is supplied.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
def adjust(value)
  if block_given?
    yield value
  else
    value
  end
end
puts adjust(3) { |value| value * 2 }
```
Expected output or behavior: 6. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Block parameters and local scope
lessons.summary: Remove ; total from the block parameter list. What prints?
explanation: A block normally sees local variables from its surrounding scope. Assigning an existing outer local inside the block can change that binding.
Names after a semicolon in the block parameter list are block-local. |value; total| keeps total local to the block even if an outer total already exists.
[1].each runs this block once with value equal to 1. The special local total does not overwrite the outer total.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
total = 10
[1].each { |value; total| total = value }
puts total
```
Expected output or behavior: 10. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Procs lambdas and arity
lessons.summary: Replace the proc with ->(value) { value } and still call it with no arguments. What happens?
explanation: proc { |value| value } makes a Proc. ->(value) { value } makes a lambda, which is also a Proc object with different calling rules.
A lambda requires its declared argument count unless defaults or rest parameters allow otherwise. This one-parameter lambda raises ArgumentError when called with no arguments.
The simple ordinary proc below accepts no arguments and binds value to nil. return inside an ordinary proc also differs from return inside a lambda; do not treat them as interchangeable.
nil.inspect returns the text nil, unlike puts nil which writes an empty line.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
reader = proc { |value| value }
puts reader.call.inspect
```
Expected output or behavior: nil. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Closures capture variable bindings
lessons.summary: Change the later assignment to offset = 20. What prints?
explanation: A proc or lambda can use an outer local variable after creation. Ruby captures the binding rather than freezing the earlier scalar value.
If offset changes from 2 to 9 before the closure is called, the closure reads 9.
Sharing a captured array also allows shared mutation. Keeping a closure can keep referenced objects reachable.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
offset = 2
add = ->(value) { value + offset }
offset = 9
puts add.call(3)
```
Expected output or behavior: 12. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

lessons.title: Safe navigation and explicit absence
lessons.summary: Replace nil with "stars". What prints?
explanation: value&.upcase calls upcase when value is not nil and returns nil without the call when value is nil. For a String, upcase returns uppercase text.
A non-nil object still must support the called method. false is not nil, so safe navigation does not skip a call on false.
result || "missing" replaces both nil and false with the fallback. That is a truthiness policy, not a universal missing-data rule.

Complete local Ruby example; the app itself does not execute it:
```ruby
value = nil
result = value&.upcase
puts result || "missing"
```
Expected output or behavior: missing. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
